text:
From US 101 at Hoodsport take North Lake Cushman Road (SR-119) about 9 miles to the T, go right on FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left on Forest Road 2419 up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to the road-end parking the standard route also uses. Park there and continue on foot: this route's way trail leaves the old roadbed roughly 1,000 ft beyond the standard route's trail entrance, just past the crossing of Big Creek at about 3,100 ft, so do not take the first trail you come to.

Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft toward the bowl below the Shield Wall. A small way trail leads to the base of the large rock section of the southeast ridge at about 3,700 ft; bear right (east) around those rocks and follow the ridgeline until you are forced right (north) by prominent gendarmes. A gully then ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's left corner at about 4,850 ft, where the technical climbing begins.

text: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.

text: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.

text: The route comprises three ridge sections separated by deep notches. The lower section is mostly class 2-4 terrain, commonly simul-climbed, staying just on the east side of the crest (harder climbing results if the crest itself is followed). After descending to the second notch, two 5.8 pitches (a dirty 5.8 chimney and a 5.8 crack pitch) lead toward the summit, separated by class 2-3 sections, with large detached blocks making protection difficult in places. A gendarme partway up offers the route's best technical climbing directly, or can be bypassed via a ~75-ft rappel to easier terrain west of the ridge.

text: The North Ridge is most commonly approached from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached by Icicle Creek Road/Eightmile Creek Road out of Leavenworth). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) along Mountaineer Creek roughly 3.5-4 miles, climbing gently through forest. Before reaching Stuart/Colchuck Lake, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path/cairned route that climbs talus benches on the slope west of the creek, staying a couple hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the creek, aiming for the Argonaut-Sherpa basin. Around 5,800 ft, the route steepens into sustained loose talus leading up to the base of the North Ridge proper (~7,000 ft), a roughly 1,500-ft-tall rock feature capped by the 8,630-ft summit. At the base, contour and work climber's-right to a lower notch, where easy slabs can be scrambled before roping up. (A southern approach via Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to Mountaineer Creek is also possible but is a longer, less direct line to this specific route.) Water is available at Mountaineer Creek but is limited higher on the talus approach - carry enough for the day. The talus benches and loose approach gully are the main hazards; expect a long, sustained boulder-hop that is more tedious than technical.

text:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead on Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake Trail along Mountaineer Creek for roughly three and a half to four miles. Before the lakes, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path and cairns climbing talus benches on the slope west of the creek — staying a couple of hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the water — aiming for the Sherpa-Argonaut basin.

Do not follow cairns out into the boulder field: parties specifically warn that the cairned line invites you off the better path. Stay with the creek.

Around 5,800 ft the ground steepens into sustained loose talus. The usual bivy is at the top of a talus field in the basin, and from there it is another hour and a half to two hours of talus-hopping to the toe of the ridge.

A southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek exists but is a longer, less direct way to this particular route.

edits.new: The usual bivy sits above a talus field in the basin

text:
Aim for the double V and camp just inside the lower one. Approaching the Sherpa-Argonaut col from the basin, the skyline reads as two V-shaped notches. The bivy sits at the top of a talus field just inside the lower V, and that pairing — two Vs, camp inside the lower — is the most reliable landmark on this approach because it is a skyline shape rather than a feature you have to be close to.

From the basin, the move is west-northwest and up a deep gully. Ascend talus west-northwest to a deep gully that runs to a notch on the ridge at about 7,000 ft. That gully is the way onto the route; contour up and climber's right out of the basin to reach the base of that lower notch.

Arrival: at the notch there are easy slabs that can be scrambled before you rope up. Easy slabs at a notch at roughly 7,000 ft, reached by a gully, with about 1,500 ft of ridge above you — that is the start.

What getting it wrong looks like, and it is expensive here: the ridge is largely Class 2-4 and you want to stay just on the east side of the crest. Straying onto the crest itself at the wrong point adds unavoidable 5.6-5.8 pitches on a route that is already long. So a party that gains the ridge somewhere other than the notch will find the climbing immediately harder than advertised — that is the signal to downclimb and traverse rather than to press on.

Confirmation low on the route: the first section ends with a roughly 25 m rappel from slings into a notch. If you have climbed a long way with no rappel, you are not on the ridge proper.

edits.new: The bivy is tucked just inside the lower V, above a talus field

text:
Esmeralda Basin / Longs Pass Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FS-9737), about 4,300 ft. Longs Pass Trail (#1229) for roughly 2.3 miles and 2,300 ft to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft.

Drop the north side, losing 1,300-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft — early season there are snow fingers here that glissade well. Ford or rock-hop the creek, join the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it right (east) about a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at about 4,700 ft.

Leave the maintained trail there. Ascend rightward across the meadow to where the slope steepens at about 5,000 ft, cross the stream, and climb the rib staying left of its crest. At around 5,800 ft traverse right, cross over the rib, and contour into the basin below Sherpa.

There is a flat table-rock shelf at about 7,400 ft that parties use as a bivy or gear-up spot. Around 6,000 ft the climbers' path enters a spot where the gully narrows; from there some parties gain a few hundred feet east to the divide separating that gully from the one leading more directly toward Sherpa, then drop grudgingly into the correct gully and take class 2 slopes up to the table rock.

Six to seven hours one way is typical. Water at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season.

text:
The landmark that settles this route is Sherpa's balanced rock — a distinctive perched block on the summit ridge, and it is visible from the basin below. Use it.

From the basin, climb class 2 snow and talus past the table rock to the Stuart-Sherpa col at about 8,100 ft, aiming for the notch closest to Sherpa. That is the start: the ridge rises east from the col to the summit, and the balanced rock stands beyond the summit on the crest to the east.

So the check in cloud is: at the col, Mount Stuart's east ridge rises behind you to the west and Sherpa's summit is ahead to the east, with the balanced rock beyond it. If you reach the crest with the balanced rock to your west, you have come up the East Ridge side of the peak.

The flat table-rock at about 7,400 ft is the intermediate confirmation on the way up — it is a distinct flat platform in otherwise broken ground and it sits on the correct line. Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

The descent uses a rappel line back to a notch west of the technical climbing, so know where the notch is before you go up.

edits.new: to the col between Stuart and Sherpa, at about 8,100 ft,

text: Park at the broad pullout/overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165–166 (about 4 miles east of Washington Pass), where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain. From the pullout, drop down the embankment roughly 150–200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log (logjams shift year to year — scout up- and downstream for the best crossing, and be ready to ford in high water/early season, when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt). On the far bank, pick up the unofficial but well-defined climber's trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From here the trail climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500–3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting creek-side water access early on — treat the crossing at Early Winters Creek as your last reliable water until camp. At around 6,000–6,400 ft the grade eases at 'the Bench,' an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby; this is the standard overnight camp for a two-day trip and a natural break point/turnaround check for day-trippers. Above the bench, continue up open subalpine terrain toward Burgundy Col. Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col — it is loose and exposed; instead stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col itself (roughly 7,800 ft). Total gain from the highway to the col is on the order of 3,500–4,400 ft depending on exact trailhead/camp used. Hazards on the approach: the Early Winters Creek crossing (cold, log can be wet/mossy or washed out), steep eroding/brushy tread that's easy to lose in the timber, and loose rock ('kitty litter') on the final gully/traverse into the col.

text:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the far side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy ramp about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

text:
The unmistakable break on this approach is the bench, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. That gully is the wrong one — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay left and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's left of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

edits.old: Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft.
edits.new: Close to the top of the gully, traverse up and to the right beneath the cliffs, crossing heather-covered slabs, to reach the col at roughly 7,800 ft.

text: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

edits.old: take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col
edits.new: go straight up the exposed Class 3+ ridge starting at the col

text: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (elev. ~1,450') on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26), follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles (easy, well-graded, mostly flat, forested trail with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek) to Sixmile Camp (2,440'), a good first-night camp with reliable water from Downey Creek. From Sixmile Camp the maintained trail ends; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek initially and fording to the south side around the 9.5-mile mark (~3,700') — treat this as a real creek crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water/early season. Around 4,500' the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone (a major slide wiped out this stretch in 2002); expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber here even in good conditions, and continuous snow well below this elevation in early season. Above the debris zone the path climbs to a pass (~5,900') just northwest of Cub Lake (about 14 miles in), then drops to Cub Lake (5,338', another good camp with water). Most parties push on from Cub Lake up onto Itswoot Ridge (6,400–6,900', ~15 miles and ~5,500' of gain from the trailhead) for high camp, with sweeping views of Dome and Sinister. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins (staying near 7,000') to gain the Dome Glacier, cross over the Dome–Chikamin col, and descend the Chikamin Glacier (crevassed — rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear) to about 7,200'. Traverse right (east) across the glacier to reach the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col; a bergschrund here can be difficult to cross in late season and has occasionally required a short rappel to get down onto or across it (see descent notes — same feature is encountered both ways). From the col, contour on an easy snowfield and climb up into a loose, unpleasant gully on Sinister's south side to gain the upper west ridge, then follow a Class 2–3 scramble along the ridge to the 8,444' summit; some parties instead take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col. Loose rock in the gully is the main climbing-specific hazard on the approach to the summit block.

edits.old: take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col
edits.new: go straight up the exposed Class 3+ ridge starting at the col

text: Reverse the ascent line. Most parties downclimb the same loose south-side gully back to the Dome–Sinister col — it is one of the loosest, most unpleasant sections on the mountain, so expect care-intensive downclimbing with real rockfall risk to anyone below. A commonly preferred alternative, used by several recent parties instead of re-descending the gully, is to descend via the lower west ridge: a newer, more direct line involving sustained Class 3–4 scrambling on semi-solid rock with considerable exposure. One crux move on this ridge variant has a fixed sling left in place for protection/handline use, but this is not a rappel station — parties downclimb through it. Either way, the descent rejoins the gentle snow slopes leading back to the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col. At the col, the bergschrund that guards access to the Chikamin Glacier can be broken/unbridged in mid-to-late season; when it is, parties have used a single rappel (one 60m rope) off natural anchors (rock horn/sling or v-thread in snow, depending on conditions) to get down onto the glacier safely rather than risk a fall into the schrund — in good snow conditions or earlier in the season this same spot is often just a step-across or short downclimb with no rope work needed. From the glacier, re-ascend roughly 1,000' back to the Dome–Chikamin col, then descend to high camp on Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and reverse the long Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully, exposure on the west-ridge variant, and crevasse hazard on the Chikamin/Dome glacier crossings in both directions.

edits.new: scrambling at Class 3–4 that stays sustained, on rock that is only partly solid

text:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.

edits.new: Around 5,800 ft you cross a small rock ridge, and the glacier first comes into view.

text: Head southwest across the glacier toward the obvious corner where the left skyline of the summit massif meets the east ridge, staying high and right on the glacier and then angling left to within about 100 ft of the east rock face. The face above sheds rock, so move left if debris is coming down and do not linger under it. Leaving the snow for rock near 7,100 ft is where the route gets awkward late in the season — the moat opens and crevasses lower on the slope may force a detour to a lower crossing. Glacier gear can be left at this transition.

text: The corkscrew itself: a rock-and-heather shelf carrying a well-worn goat and climber path that cuts high across the entire south face, around the corner and partway onto the west face. The tread is good and the scrambling easy, but above roughly 7,200 ft the ledge is edged by a drop of around 500 ft, so this is the section where a slip is not survivable despite the modest grade. Wet or frosted heather and lingering snow patches on the shelf are the thing to watch.

text: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead (~1,150-1,200 ft, a signed gravel pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, about 21 miles east of Marblemount just past the Diablo turnoff), follow the well-maintained Pyramid Lake Trail as it climbs steadily through old-growth forest. A rock-hop creek crossing at roughly 1 mile is the last easy, reliable water before the lake. At 2.1 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain you reach Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft) - top off water here, since the next several hours offer little. From the lake's south/right side, pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' path; it is steep and brushy from the outset and gains roughly 2,000 ft more, switchbacking up to the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak (~4,000 ft), then follows the narrow, knolly ridge crest past Point 4,555 ft toward Pyramid Peak, with loose rock and short routefinding steps. Just short of Pyramid Peak, descend slightly and traverse - often on lingering snow - across scree and boulders to the terminal moraine and small lake at the base of the Colonial Glacier (~5,900-6,100 ft), the standard first camp, with a tarn for water. From camp, rope up for glacier travel (crevasses present) and climb the Colonial Glacier south to the broad Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,900 ft; a stream/waterfall here is a second good camp and water source), then descend about 200 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it - a moderate, usually well-tracked but crevassed glacier crossing requiring a rope - to the rocks just below Snowfield's summit pyramid on its northwest side. From there a long class 3 gully leads to a notch below the true summit; the final short traverse/scramble across the notch to the south side and up to the summit (8,351 ft) is exposed class 3, with one move occasionally rated low class 4. Given roughly 7,300 ft of total gain and sustained glacier travel, most parties treat this as a 2-day (overnight) objective rather than a single push.

text:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.

text:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.

text:
Two tests, one at the gully fork and one at the wall, and you need both.

First, the fork at about 7,100 ft. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the left branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

Second, the wall itself, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are two short left-facing corners side by side. The route starts in the rightmost and larger of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

What the climbing should feel like, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is not evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A separate feature worth not confusing with the start: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and the approach description on this route describes it as though it were the route. It is not the base of the 5.6 face climb, and a party navigating to it will end up on the scramble.

edits.old: The route starts in the rightmost and larger of the two.
edits.new: The route begins in the right-hand corner, the larger one of the pair.
